pages.text: The body destroys anomalous cells all the time. A tumour exists because it escaped. $(thing)Immune evasion$(): it sheds the markers T cells look for, shows PD-L1 to switch them off, and recruits cells that suppress inflammation. $(thing)Immortality$(): every division shortens the telomeres at the chromosome ends until a cell must stop - unless it switches $(thing)telomerase$() back on.

$(thing)Angiogenesis$(): beyond a millimetre it starves, so it calls in new blood vessels (VEGF). Even then it slows: a tumour grows as N = K·exp(ln(N₀/K)e^{−αt}), fast when small and levelling off at the capacity of its supply. $(thing)Metastasis$(): cells loosen their grip (the epithelial-mesenchymal transition), enter the blood, survive the journey and grow again elsewhere. Most die; it only takes one.

In the $(item)Bioreactor$(): a strain culture with a telomerase complex becomes an $(item)Immortal Cell Line$() - and an immortal line in broth is passaged into twelve, forever. In the $(item)Evolution Engine$(): an immortal line and a silicon spore in xenoplasm make $(item)Metastatic Spores$().
Telomerase switched back on: the chromosome ends rebuild themselves, and the cells forget how to grow old. They have outlived their donor.$(br2)Made in $(item)Bioreactor$().
A cluster of cells that has learned to leave: to slip its tissue, ride the blood and grow again somewhere it was never meant to be.$(br2)Made in $(item)Evolution Engine$().
